html:
The cocoliztli epidemics were outbreaks of a deadly fever with bleeding that swept the Mexican highlands of New Spain, above all in 1545 to 1548 and again in 1576. They are often called the worst epidemics in Mexico's history.

Cocoliztli is the Nahuatl word for "pestilence". Victims had high fever, headaches, bleeding from the nose and mouth, and often died within days. The outbreak of 1545 is estimated to have killed between 5 and 15 million people, perhaps most of the Indigenous people of the region. It came only a generation after smallpox had struck during the conquest, so it fell on a population already shattered.

What caused it is still debated. Spanish and Indigenous doctors at the time could not identify it. In 2018 a study of DNA from victims buried at a cemetery in Oaxaca found a strain of Salmonella that causes a form of enteric fever, and suggested it was at least partly to blame. Others think it was a native viral fever, made worse by the region's worst droughts in centuries and by the hard conditions of forced labour after the conquest.

The deaths changed colonial society. With fewer Indigenous workers, Spanish landowners and mine owners turned more to forced labour drafts and to enslaved Africans brought by the Atlantic slave trade. Together with smallpox and measles, the epidemics were part of the great dying that followed the Columbian Exchange across the Americas.
